title: Watercolour Supplies for Beginners, Without the Muddy Paintings
dek: Ten watercolour supplies ranked by how much better your paintings get. Spend on paper first; it matters more than paint.
seo_title: Paper matters more than paint. Ten watercolour supplies ranked by how much they improve a beginner's results, from cotton paper to a good round brush.
hero_image: a watercolour palette, brushes and a half-finished landscape painting
intro: Beginners usually buy watercolour supplies backwards. They get a big set of cheap paints, a pad of thin paper and a bundle of stiff brushes. Then the paper buckles and pills, the colours turn to mud and the brushes will not hold a point. They decide they are bad at painting, when the materials were fighting them the whole time.
This list is ordered by how much each item improves your results. Paper first, then a few good brushes, then paint. A small, well-chosen kit beats a giant cheap one, and it costs about the same.

Prices below are approximate street prices at the time of writing and move around constantly, especially during sale events. Treat them as a rough band for budgeting, not a quote. Always check the live listing before you buy.
how_we_pick: These picks come from art teachers' recommendations, painting communities and long-run owner reports, cross-checked against current retail listings. We have not personally tested every item here. Art supplies are widely counterfeited on marketplaces, so buy branded paints and papers from official stores.

products.name: 100% cotton watercolour paper, 140lb (300gsm)
products.image: a block of cotton watercolour paper with a wash painted on it
products.body: Paper is where watercolour succeeds or fails. Cheap wood-pulp paper absorbs paint unevenly, buckles and pills when you rework it. Cotton paper holds water evenly, lets colours flow and blend, and survives lifting and layering. Arches, Baohong and Fabriano Artistico are well-known cotton papers. It costs more per sheet, so cut large sheets into quarters for practice. This single change does more for beginners than any other. The case for it: colours blend and flow properly, survives reworking, and makes techniques actually work. The trade-off is real: expensive per sheet and fakes exist; buy from official stores, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used.
cons: Fakes exist; buy from official stores

products.name: A size 8-10 round brush with a good point
products.tag: The one brush that does most
products.search: size 8-10 round brush with a good point
products.image: a round watercolour brush with a fine point
products.body: A good round brush holds a lot of water and still makes a fine point, so one brush can paint a wash and a thin line. Synthetic brushes designed to mimic sable are affordable and good. Test the point: dip in water, flick, and it should snap back to a sharp tip. You can paint almost everything with this one brush. The case for it: does washes and details, holds plenty of water, and lasts for years with care. The trade-off is real: good brushes need care and never leave standing in water, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used.

products.name: A student-grade pan set with 12 colours
products.image: a compact watercolour pan set with 12 colours
products.body: A small pan set from a known brand, such as Winsor and Newton Cotman, Sakura Koi or similar, gives good colour for a low price. Twelve colours is plenty; more colours encourage muddy mixing. Pans travel well and last a long time. The case for it: affordable decent colour, portable, and lasts a long time. The trade-off is real: less vivid than artist-grade paint and large cheap sets are mostly filler, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. Priced around $15-35, it is easy to justify even if it only ends up getting occasional rather than daily use.
cons: Large cheap sets are mostly filler

products.name: A flat wash brush
products.image: a flat brush laying down a sky wash
products.body: A 1-inch flat brush lays down smooth washes for skies, water and backgrounds quickly. It also makes crisp edges for buildings. Synthetic is fine. The case for it: fast, even washes, crisp edges, and cheap. The trade-off is real: less useful for detail and cheap ones shed hairs, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. At $10-20, it earns its place on this list without asking for a big up-front commitment either way. As with anything on this list, check the exact listing details and current price before adding it to a cart.

products.name: A water brush pen
products.image: a water brush pen being used in a sketchbook outdoors
products.body: A water brush has a hollow barrel you fill with water, so there is no water cup to carry. It is perfect for sketching outdoors, travel and urban sketching. Pentel and Sakura make popular ones. A set with several tip sizes is cheap. The case for it: no water cup needed, great for travel, and cheap. The trade-off is real: harder to control water flow and tips wear out, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. For $8-15, it is a small, low-risk addition to the list rather than a centrepiece purchase you need to think hard about.

products.name: Masking tape
products.image: masking tape holding watercolour paper to a board
products.body: Taping paper to a board on all sides reduces buckling as it dries and leaves a clean white border. Use low-tack artist tape and peel slowly when the painting is fully dry, at an angle, to avoid tearing. The case for it: reduces buckling, clean borders, and cheap. The trade-off is real: can tear paper if removed too fast and regular tape can be too sticky, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. Priced around $5-10, it is easy to justify even if it only ends up getting occasional rather than daily use.
cons: Can tear paper if removed too fast
Regular tape can be too sticky

products.name: A porcelain or plastic mixing palette
products.image: a white porcelain mixing palette with colours
products.body: A white palette with wells gives you space to mix colours and see them accurately. Porcelain lets paint bead less and cleans easily; plastic is cheaper and lighter. A white ceramic plate works too. The case for it: accurate colour mixing, easy to clean, and cheap. The trade-off is real: porcelain breaks and plastic stains over time, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. At $8-20, it earns its place on this list without asking for a big up-front commitment either way. As with anything on this list, check the exact listing details and current price before adding it to a cart.

products.name: A few artist-grade tubes
products.body: Once you are painting regularly, a few artist-grade colours add brightness and mix cleaner. A warm and cool version of each primary colour, six tubes, covers almost everything. Squeeze into an empty palette and let them dry into pans. The case for it: brighter, cleaner colour, last a long time, and mix more predictably. The trade-off is real: expensive per tube and some pigments are toxic; avoid ingesting, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. For $10-15 each, it is a small, low-risk addition to the list rather than a centrepiece purchase you need to think hard about.
cons: Some pigments are toxic; avoid ingesting

products.name: A travel sketchbook for watercolour
products.image: an open watercolour sketchbook with small paintings
products.body: A sketchbook with watercolour-weight paper is where most improvement happens: small, quick daily paintings. It also becomes a lovely travel journal. Look for 140lb paper in a book that lies flat. The case for it: encourages daily practice, travel journal, and portable. The trade-off is real: pages buckle a bit and cotton sketchbooks are expensive, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. Priced around $15-25, it is easy to justify even if it only ends up getting occasional rather than daily use. None of that makes it essential for everyone reading this, only worth knowing about if the description above matches how you actually use the space.

products.name: Masking fluid
products.image: masking fluid applied to paper to keep white highlights
products.body: There is no white paint in traditional watercolour; the white is the paper. Masking fluid protects small areas, like highlights or snowflakes, so you can paint freely around them and rub it off later. Use an old brush; it ruins good ones. The case for it: keeps crisp whites, allows loose painting, and a little goes a long way. The trade-off is real: ruins good brushes and can tear cheap paper when removed, so weigh that against how often it would actually get used. At $10-15, it earns its place on this list without asking for a big up-front commitment either way.
pros: A little goes a long way
cons: Can tear cheap paper when removed

faq.q: What watercolour supplies should a beginner buy first?
faq.a: Cotton paper, one good round brush and a small student-grade paint set.

faq.q: Why do my paintings look muddy?
faq.a: Often cheap paper, too many layers, or mixing too many colours. Let layers dry fully and mix no more than two or three colours.
Pans are easier and portable. Tubes give more paint for larger work.

faq.q: Is cotton paper really worth it?
faq.a: Yes. It is the biggest single improvement in watercolour.
